records.name: Dutch West India Company (WIC)
records.scaleNote: Dutch-flagged ships carried c. 550,000 captives across the Atlantic (per SlaveVoyages via the African Studies Centre Leiden), and the WIC held the Dutch monopoly on that trade until 1730.
records.origins: Chartered by the States General in 1621 as a joint-stock company with a monopoly on Dutch trade and war in the Atlantic, organised in regional chambers (Amsterdam, Zeeland, Maas and others). Its first aims were privateering against Spain and Portugal and seizing Portuguese sugar lands in Brazil; it entered the slave trade to supply Dutch Brazil.
records.role_summary: Between 1637 and 1641 the WIC seized Portuguese slaving posts at Elmina, São Tomé and Luanda, making the Republic a leading slave-trading power. After losing Brazil in 1654 it turned Curaçao into a slave entrepôt supplying Spanish America under asiento sub-contracts, and it shipped captives to Suriname, New Netherland and other colonies.

roleDetail.d: WIC forces took São Jorge da Mina from the Portuguese in August 1637; it became the WIC's West African headquarters for gold and slave trading into the 19th century.

Taking Luanda gave the WIC direct access to the Angolan slave supply for Brazil, and it allied with Queen Nzinga of Ndongo-Matamba against Portugal until Portuguese-Brazilian forces retook the city in 1648.

roleDetail.t: Made Curaçao a regional slave market.
roleDetail.d: Curaçao was the dominant Dutch distribution centre for captives sold on to Spanish colonies before the mid-18th century, later overtaken by Sint Eustatius (per SlaveVoyages notes on the intra-American trade).
The company owned most of the enslaved Africans in New Amsterdam from c. 1626, using them on public works; in 1644 eleven men won 'half-freedom' after nearly two decades of forced labour.

records.legacy: The WIC lost its slave-trade monopoly in 1730 and was dissolved in 1791, when its possessions passed to the Dutch state. Its history underlies the Dutch state's 2022 apology, King Willem-Alexander's 2023 apology, and the 2022 programme marking 400 years since its founding.

legacyDetail.d: PM Mark Rutte apologised on 19 December 2022 for the Dutch state's role in slavery and announced a €200 million awareness fund, rejecting individual reparations.
WIC records in the Nationaal Archief in The Hague underpin modern voyage databases, including Curaçao slave trade records for 1700–1730.

records.name: Middelburgsche Commercie Compagnie (MCC)
records.scaleNote: The largest Dutch slave trader after 1730: it bought 31,095 enslaved Africans between 1732 and 1803 for sale in the Caribbean and Suriname (per Zeeuws Archief/MCC records).
records.origins: Founded in Middelburg in 1720 as a general trading company. When the WIC lost its monopoly on the Dutch Atlantic slave trade in 1730, the MCC moved into 'free' slave trading and by the 1740s was the leading Dutch slaver.
records.role_summary: The MCC sent triangular voyages from Zeeland to the West African coast (Gold Coast, Loango and elsewhere) and on to Suriname, Curaçao and Sint Eustatius, selling captives for plantation produce. Between 1756 and 1807 it sent out 92 triangular voyages and 22 other voyages.

roleDetail.d: Company records count 31,095 enslaved Africans bought from 1732 to 1803, carried on ships such as the Eenigheid (Unity, 1761–1763).

Logbooks, surgeons' journals, ledgers and letters survive in the Zeeuws Archief and are on UNESCO's Memory of the World Register. They record trade in detail, but the captives themselves are mostly anonymous.

records.legacy: The MCC stopped slave trading after the British and Dutch bans of the early 19th century and was dissolved in 1889. Its papers passed to the Zeeland archives; online projects such as 'Slavenhandel MCC' now reconstruct individual voyages for the public.

legacyDetail.d: The MCC archive was inscribed for its detail and condition, making it one of the best-documented slave-trading archives anywhere.

records.name: House of Orange-Nassau (stadholders and monarchs)
records.scaleNote: A 2023 government-commissioned study ('Staat en Slavernij') estimated stadholders Willem III–V drew c. €545 million (today's value) from colonial roles and VOC/WIC payments in 1675–1770; the royal-commissioned Leiden study presented on 2 October 2026 estimated c. €576 million (some outlets round to c. €500 million) in colonial income over 1600–present, mostly from the Dutch East Indies, and 'almost nothing' from the slave trade itself.
records.origins: The princes of Orange led the Dutch Revolt against Spain and served as stadholders of the Republic. Their political leadership made them patrons and beneficiaries of the VOC and WIC.
records.role_summary: Stadholders received payments from the WIC and VOC, and from 1748/49 held the title of chief director of both companies. As kings after 1815 they presided over a state that kept slavery in Suriname and the Antilles until 1863.

roleDetail.d: Per the 2023 'Staat en Slavernij' research by Raymund Schütz, shareholders arranged to pay the Oranges as if they held c. 3% of shares; Willem III's VOC share alone was c. 1.09 million guilders.

roleDetail.t: Contested weight in the Atlantic trade.
roleDetail.d: The royal-commissioned Leiden study (led by Gert Oostindie, presented 2 Oct 2026) found the family earned almost nothing directly from the slave trade, but supported colonialism, including slavery, 'wholeheartedly' and shares responsibility for its survival; monarchs rarely shaped colonial policy directly. The 2023 and 2026 studies use different periods and methods.

records.legacy: On 1 July 2023 (Keti Koti, 160 years after the 1863 abolition), King Willem-Alexander apologised in Amsterdam for the Netherlands' role in slavery and said the monarchs of the House of Orange 'took no steps against it'. He commissioned independent research into the family's colonial income, published in 2026.

legacyDetail.d: The king called slavery a crime against humanity and asked forgiveness for his ancestors' part in it; the government still ruled out reparations.

Leiden researchers (presented 2 October 2026) estimated c. €576 million in colonial earnings from 1600 to the present, mostly from the Dutch East Indies; the king called the findings 'painful and confronting'.

records.name: De Nederlandsche Bank (DNB)
records.scaleNote: Leiden University research found part of DNB's start-up capital came from slavery-linked investors and that board members held enslaved people; DNB also handled 1863 compensation payments to enslavers.
records.origins: Founded in 1814 by King Willem I as a private note-issuing bank to rebuild Dutch finance after French rule. Its founding shareholders and directors included merchants with plantation and slave-economy interests.
records.role_summary: DNB acknowledged involvement in slavery between 1814 and 1863. It financed trade linked to slave-produced goods, had directors who were enslavers, and was involved in paying compensation to plantation owners when slavery was abolished in 1863.

roleDetail.d: An independent Leiden University study (2022) found several board members were personally involved in slavery.
At abolition in 1863 the Dutch state paid enslavers per person freed, not the freed people, and DNB was involved in those payments, including to its own board members.

records.legacy: President Klaas Knot apologised on 1 July 2022 (Keti Koti). DNB set up a €5 million fund with the Cultuurfonds for initiatives led by descendants of enslaved people, plus €5 million for education and heritage projects.

legacyDetail.d: DNB apologised publicly, created two €5 million funds and pledged support to the national research centre on slavery history.

records.name: ABN AMRO (predecessors Hope & Co. and R. Mees & Zoonen)
records.scaleNote: IISH research found c. 25–33% of predecessor Hope & Co.'s revenue in sample years (1770, 1790) came from slavery, and that it was financially involved in at least 73 Caribbean plantations; Mees & Zoonen arranged at least 16 insurance policies on slave ships.
records.origins: ABN AMRO is the product of many mergers. Its legal predecessors include the Amsterdam merchant bank Hope & Co. (a major 18th-century international house) and the Rotterdam firm R. Mees & Zoonen.
records.role_summary: Hope & Co. lent to plantation owners in Dutch, British and Danish colonies with enslaved people as security, traded slave-produced goods and sometimes pushed plantation managers to buy or sell enslaved people. Mees & Zoonen insured captives aboard slave ships.

roleDetail.d: Hope & Co. financed at least 73 Caribbean plantations and was involved in their day-to-day management (IISH, 2022).
R. Mees & Zoonen arranged insurance on enslaved people carried on ships, and partners invested in Rotterdam funds for Suriname plantations.

records.legacy: After commissioning research from the International Institute of Social History, ABN AMRO apologised in April 2022 for its predecessors' role, while declining to pay reparations.

legacyDetail.d: CEO Robert Swaak apologised for 'the pain and suffering' caused; the bank said it would fund awareness projects, not reparations.

records.name: Coymans family (Balthasar Coymans)
records.scaleNote: Balthasar Coymans's 1685 asiento obliged him to deliver more than 22,000 enslaved people to Spanish America within 4.5 years (per Ramona Negrón's research); the contract largely failed.
records.origins: A Flemish-Dutch merchant dynasty with branches in Amsterdam, Haarlem and Cádiz that traded silver, spices and textiles with the Spanish Americas.
records.role_summary: In 1685 Balthasar Coymans obtained the Spanish asiento de negros, the licence to supply enslaved Africans to Spanish America. He relied on the WIC to buy captives and on Curaçao as the depot, sending agents across the Caribbean.

roleDetail.d: The contract put the Spanish slave supply in Dutch hands; evidence for it survives in archives in the Netherlands, Spain, Curaçao, Jamaica, Colombia, Cuba, Mexico and Panama.
Coymans died in 1686 and the contract ended in disputes with Spain; one effect was that captives held on Curaçao 'piled up' unsold.

records.legacy: The family's role is the subject of new scholarship (Negrón's Leiden dissertation and a Routledge book) on Dutch entrepreneurs who worked inside other empires' slave systems.

legacyDetail.d: Historians now use the Coymans case to show how Dutch capital served the Spanish slave trade.

records.name: Van Aerssen van Sommelsdijck family
records.scaleNote: One-third owners of the Society of Suriname (1683–1770); by 1713 the colony had c. 200 plantations worked by c. 13,000 enslaved Africans.
records.origins: A Dutch noble family. Cornelis van Aerssen van Sommelsdijck bought a one-third share of the new Society of Suriname in 1683, alongside the city of Amsterdam and the WIC.
records.role_summary: Cornelis became the colony's first governor under the Society and expanded plantations and repression of Maroon communities; he was killed by mutinous soldiers in 1688. The family kept its third share until selling it in 1770.

roleDetail.d: He ran a colony whose sugar, coffee and cocoa were produced by enslaved Africans and shipped to Amsterdam.
The family sold its share for c. 700,000 guilders.

records.legacy: Fort Sommelsdijk in Suriname bears the family's name. Their stake shows how noble families shared directly in colonial plantation profits alongside cities and companies.

legacyDetail.d: Fort Sommelsdijk, at the meeting of the Commewijne and Cottica rivers, was built under Cornelis's governorship.

records.name: Compagnie des Indes (French Indies Company)
records.scaleNote: Held the French slave-trade monopoly for Senegal from 1718 and for Guinea in the 1720s; it carried the first captives to Louisiana (1719), where 23 voyages landed c. 6,235 Africans by 1769 (per SlaveVoyages), but sent only c. 16% of French slave ships in 1720–1749.
records.origins: Formed from John Law's Compagnie d'Occident (1717), which absorbed the earlier Senegal and Guinea companies and the East India Company to become the Compagnie des Indes in 1719. It was tied to Law's bank and the 'Mississippi bubble'.
records.role_summary: The company held legal monopolies on French slave trading in West Africa and on Louisiana's trade, running forts at Saint-Louis, Gorée and Ouidah. In practice private shipowners from Nantes and other ports did most French slave trading under licence.

roleDetail.d: The company ship Duc du Maine landed the first African captives in Louisiana on 6 June 1719, from Senegambia.
Between 1723 and 1725 Lorient was among the first slave ports of France, per the French Service historique de la Défense.
A study of the Ouidah trade finds the company sent only 16.1% of French slave ships in 1720–1749, so its legal monopoly overstated its actual role.

records.legacy: Louisiana returned to the Crown in 1731 and the company lost its monopoly in 1769; it was finally wound up in the Revolution. Lorient, the city it founded, keeps its history in the Musée de la Compagnie des Indes in Port-Louis.

legacyDetail.t: A city built by the company.
legacyDetail.d: Lorient takes its name from the company's port (L'Orient) and the Port-Louis citadel houses a museum of the company.

records.name: Montaudoin family (Montaudouin)
records.scaleNote: Among Nantes's leading slave-trading houses for much of the 18th century; one secondary source credits the family with 357 ships, though voyage counts vary between sources.
records.origins: A Nantes merchant family whose outfitting firm, René Montaudouin et consors, operated from 1698 to 1730. Two branches were ennobled in 1750 by buying offices of royal secretary.
records.role_summary: The Montaudoins outfitted slave ships to West Africa and sold captives in the French Caribbean, especially Saint-Domingue and Martinique. René Montaudoin owned La Concorde, which made slaving voyages in 1713–14, 1715–16 and 1717 before pirates seized it and it became Blackbeard's Queen Anne's Revenge.

roleDetail.d: On its third voyage La Concorde embarked 516 captives at Ouidah (Juda); 61 died in the crossing, and it was seized by Blackbeard's pirates on 28 November 1717 near Martinique with 455 captives aboard. Renamed Queen Anne's Revenge, it ran aground off Beaufort, North Carolina, in June 1718; the wreck is being excavated.
The family continued large-scale outfitting until the eve of the Revolution; Jean-Gabriel Montaudoüin de La Touche corresponded with Benjamin Franklin.

records.role_summary: Gradis ships left Bordeaux with goods, bought captives at Gorée and sold them in the Caribbean. Abraham Gradis supplied the Crown in Canada and West Africa; in the 1760s his West African contracts were paid partly in enslaved people, who were sold in Saint-Domingue for sugar.

roleDetail.d: The house set up on Gorée to buy captives for the Americas.
Abraham Gradis was a major supplier to French colonial forces, linking the firm closely to royal policy.

records.origins: A Protestant merchant family of Bordeaux, with Jean-Baptiste Nairac (1738–1817) active as a shipowner in La Rochelle. They owned sugar refineries in Bordeaux's Sainte-Croix district.
records.role_summary: The Nairacs sent slave ships to the Bight of Benin and other coasts and sold captives in Saint-Domingue, while refining the sugar enslaved people produced.

roleDetail.d: SlaveVoyages records a Nairac ship sailing from La Rochelle in 1771 to the Bight of Benin and Saint-Domingue, and Paul Nairac voyages from Bordeaux.
Combining slaving voyages with sugar refining let the family profit at both ends of the triangle.

records.legacy: Their Bordeaux mansions and refinery sites are part of the city's colonial-heritage tours; the Musée d'Aquitaine covers Bordeaux's slave trade in rooms opened in 2009.

legacyDetail.d: The family is among the Bordeaux houses named in the city's remembrance of the slave trade.

records.today: Historical descendants include Guillaume Jean Jacques Nairac (1787–1845), a Dutch politician from another branch, and Édouard Nairac (1876–1960), a Mauritian politician. The family received compensation in 1826 for its Saint-Domingue plantations. The Hôtel Nairac in Bordeaux and the Château Nairac in Barsac, sold by the heirs in 1837, survive, and the family's correspondence is a key source for historians of the Bordeaux slave trade.

records.name: Crown of France (Bourbon monarchy)
records.scaleNote: French-flagged ships embarked c. 1.38 million captives (SlaveVoyages estimates, 1501–1866: 1,381,404, c. 11% of the Atlantic total), all under royal charters, licences and law; by 1789 Saint-Domingue alone held c. 465,000 enslaved people.
records.lifespan: 1664–1848 (colonial slavery under the Crown and successor regimes)
records.origins: Under Louis XIV and his minister Colbert, the Crown built a colonial system in the Caribbean and chartered companies to supply it with enslaved Africans.
records.role_summary: The Crown chartered the Senegal, Guinea and Indies companies, issued the Code Noir (1685) and in 1701 won the Spanish asiento for the Compagnie de Guinée. In 1825 Charles X forced Haiti to pay a 150 million franc indemnity for France's recognition.

roleDetail.d: The 1685 Code Noir, issued at Versailles, regulated slavery in French colonies and stayed largely in force until 1848.
Charles X's 1825 ordinance, backed by warships, made recognition of Haiti conditional on 150 million francs to compensate former colonists, including for enslaved 'property'.
After the Republic abolished slavery in 1794, Napoleon restored it in 1802; it was finally abolished on 27 April 1848.

records.legacy: The 2001 Taubira Law declared the slave trade and slavery a crime against humanity. In April 2025 President Macron set up a joint Franco-Haitian commission of historians on the 1825 debt, without accepting reparations.

legacyDetail.d: A law of 30 April 1849 paid former owners 126 million francs over 20 years; freed people received nothing.
Haitian governments and campaigners continue to seek restitution of the indemnity; France has not agreed to repay it.

records.name: Danish West India-Guinea Company
records.scaleNote: Ran Denmark-Norway's Gold Coast forts and Caribbean colonies from 1674 to 1755; ships under the Danish/Baltic flag embarked c. 111,000 captives in all, of whom c. 92,000 survived to disembark (SlaveVoyages estimates, 1501–1866).
records.origins: Chartered by King Christian V in 1671 to colonise St Thomas; it took over the Guinea trade and became the West India-Guinea Company. Its Gold Coast base was Christiansborg at Osu (Accra), taken from the Swedes in the late 1650s.
records.role_summary: The company bought captives at Christiansborg and other Gold Coast posts and shipped them to St Thomas, St John (from 1718) and St Croix (bought from France in 1733), where enslaved people worked sugar plantations. It also leased part of St Thomas to the Brandenburg company.

roleDetail.d: From 1674 to 1755 the company administered the Danish settlements in Guinea and supplied the Danish West Indies with captives.
Enslaved Akwamu people on St John rose against company rule in 1733 and held the island for months before French troops suppressed them.

records.legacy: The Crown took over the colonies in 1754–55. Denmark sold its Gold Coast forts to Britain in 1850 and the Danish West Indies to the United States in 1917; the 2017 centenary set off Denmark's largest public reckoning with its colonial past.

legacyDetail.d: Nearly 30 exhibitions marked 100 years since the sale of the islands; PM Lars Løkke Rasmussen called the era 'shameful' but no formal apology followed.

records.name: Schimmelmann family (Heinrich Carl & Ernst von Schimmelmann)
records.scaleNote: Heinrich Carl von Schimmelmann was the largest Danish slave owner and trader, with over 1,000 enslaved people on four plantations in the Danish West Indies.
records.origins: Heinrich Carl, a Prussian-born merchant and war profiteer, entered Danish service as treasurer and was made a count. In 1763 he bought the king's four West Indian plantations on favourable terms, along with a Copenhagen sugar refinery and slave ships.
records.role_summary: Schimmelmann linked guns and textiles from his factories, slaving voyages from the Gold Coast, Caribbean sugar plantations and his Copenhagen refinery into one circuit. His son Ernst, as finance minister, chaired the commission behind the 1792 Danish slave-trade ban while the family kept its plantations.

roleDetail.d: He tied his estates and factories into a closed loop between Western Europe, West Africa and the Caribbean.
Ernst Schimmelmann chaired the 1791 Slave Trade Commission; the ten-year delay he backed let planters build up their enslaved workforce first.

records.legacy: The fortune was locked in an entail for the family. A bust of Heinrich Carl erected in Hamburg-Wandsbek in 2006 was paint-attacked and removed in 2008 after two years of protest, though streets there still bear his name.

legacyDetail.d: The Wandsbek bust became a test case in Germany's debate over honouring slave traders.
Hans Jonathan, born enslaved in 1784 on St Croix and brought to Copenhagen by the family, lost a 1802 freedom suit and fled to Iceland.

records.lifespan: 1658–1848 (slavery under the Crown); colonies sold 1850 and 1917
records.origins: Denmark-Norway entered the Gold Coast trade in the 1650s with the help of ex-Swedish agent Hendrik Carloff and chartered a West India company in 1671.
records.role_summary: The Crown chartered the companies, bought St Croix from France in 1733, ran the colonies directly from 1755 and sold royal plantations to Schimmelmann in 1763. King Christian VII signed the decree of 16 March 1792 banning the trade, effective 1803.

roleDetail.d: The 1792 decree was among the first national bans on the Atlantic slave trade, but its ten-year delay increased imports in the meantime.
On 3 July 1848 enslaved people on St Croix led by 'General Buddhoe' rose up; Governor-General Peter von Scholten then proclaimed emancipation.

records.legacy: Denmark sold the islands to the US in 1917 for $25 million. During the 2017 centenary the Danish government acknowledged the 'shameful' past but did not formally apologise; Ghana and USVI groups continue to press for reparations.

legacyDetail.d: Denmark's National Museum notes that Danes credit von Scholten with emancipation, while Virgin Islanders credit the enslaved themselves.

records.name: Brandenburg African Company
records.scaleNote: The University of Potsdam estimates c. 30,000 people were deported through Brandenburg's trade from the West African coast; the company was never profitable for long.
records.origins: Founded in 1682 by Elector Frederick William on the advice of his Dutch naval director Benjamin Raule, as a joint-stock venture promising investors a share of profits. Its seat moved to Emden in 1683.
records.role_summary: Gold proved scarce, so the company's Gold Coast forts, led by Groß Friedrichsburg, came to focus on buying captives. From 1685 it leased land on Danish St Thomas to sell them in the Caribbean, and it also held Arguin off Mauritania.

roleDetail.d: Raule agreed with the Danish company to use land on St Thomas for trade, mainly in enslaved people; the Danes seized the Brandenburg section in 1693.

legacyDetail.d: Groß Friedrichsburg passed to the WIC, which renamed it Fort Hollandia.

records.today: Frederick William's direct descendants form the House of Hohenzollern, whose head, Georg Friedrich, Prince of Prussia, is a public figure known mainly for the family's restitution disputes with the German state. No public statement by the family on Brandenburg's slave trade has been documented. In Potsdam, postcolonial initiatives and the university now cover the Elector's African ventures.

today_people.name: Georg Friedrich, Prince of Prussia
today_people.relation: head of the House of Hohenzollern, direct descendant of Elector Frederick William
today_people.role: Head of the former royal house; known for restitution claims against the German state (partly withdrawn 2023); no statement on Brandenburg's slave trade

records.name: Benjamin Raule
records.scaleNote: Organised Brandenburg's Guinea and Caribbean slave trade, which deported c. 30,000 people in total.
records.origins: A Zeeland (Dutch) shipowner and privateer who entered Brandenburg's service, becoming director-general of the Elector's navy.
records.role_summary: Raule organised the expedition that founded Groß Friedrichsburg, ran the Brandenburg African Company and negotiated the 1685 St Thomas lease with Denmark for selling captives. He was dismissed and imprisoned after the Elector's death in 1688 on corruption charges.

roleDetail.t: Dutch know-how for a German state.
roleDetail.d: Raule brought Dutch shipping and slave-trading expertise to Brandenburg.
He signed the November 1685 agreement with the Danish company.

records.legacy: Raule is remembered in German naval history as founder of the Brandenburg navy; his role in the slave trade is now part of colonial-memory debates.

legacyDetail.d: He is often celebrated in German naval tradition with little attention to the slave trade.

lineage.name: Zeeland merchant shipping
lineage.note: Raule began as a Dutch merchant and privateer outfitter in Zeeland before entering Brandenburg service.

lineage.name: Frederick William, the Great Elector
lineage.note: Made him director of the navy and backed his 1680–81 Guinea expedition and the 1682 company.

lineage.name: Otto Friedrich von der Groeben
lineage.note: Led the company fleet that founded Groß Friedrichsburg under Raule's direction.

lineage.name: Brandenburg African Company
lineage.note: Raule ran it and in 1685 arranged the St Thomas lease with Denmark for selling captives.

lineage.name: Frederick III/I
lineage.note: Raule lost favour under the Great Elector's son and was arrested on charges of corruption.

records.today: No publicly documented descendants have been traced. Raule's fortune was largely lost after his fall, and his public memory is now as the founder of the Brandenburg navy and a figure in German colonial-memory debates.

records.name: Swedish Africa Company
records.scaleNote: A short-lived company (1649–1663) whose Gold Coast posts traded mainly gold and ivory, with limited slave trading; it was soon displaced by Denmark and the Dutch.
records.origins: Founded in 1649 under a charter from Queen Christina by Louis De Geer and his son Laurens, with ex-WIC official Hendrik Carloff as its African expert.
records.role_summary: Carloff's 1650 expedition built Carolusborg at Cabo Corso (Cape Coast) with the permission of the king of Fetu. The company traded on the Gold Coast until the Danes took Carolusborg in 1658 and the Dutch the remaining posts in 1663.

roleDetail.d: The fort became Cape Coast Castle, later Britain's West African headquarters.
Sweden's direct role in the Atlantic slave trade through this company was small; its scale is debated.

records.legacy: Sweden later held Saint-Barthélemy (1784–1878) and used it as a free port, including for trade in enslaved people, before abolishing slavery there in 1847. Swedish museums now cover this history.

legacyDetail.d: Sweden's Caribbean colony held enslaved people until 1847.

lineage.name: 1646 De Geer expedition
lineage.note: A De Geer-backed voyage to West Africa returned with sugar, gold, ivory and enslaved Africans.

lineage.name: Louis & Laurens De Geer
lineage.note: Set up the company under Queen Christina's charter; Laurens signed its Amsterdam contracts, including the hiring of Carloff.

lineage.name: Hendrik Carloff
lineage.note: Built Carolusborg and ran the Gold Coast posts until he deserted to Denmark in 1657.

lineage.name: Dutch West India Company
lineage.note: Took the remaining Swedish posts. After the WIC paid damages to the Swedes, the company was formally abolished in 1663.

lineage.name: Swedish Crown / Saint-Barthélemy
lineage.note: Sweden re-entered the Atlantic slavery economy through Saint-Barthélemy and the Swedish West India Company (1786–1805), and abolished slavery there in 1847.

records.today: The company has no surviving successor; its interests ended with the 1663 settlement. Responsibility for Sweden's colonial past rests with the Swedish state, which has not formally apologised. The founding De Geer family remains a prominent noble family in Sweden.

today_people.name: Carl Johan De Geer
today_people.relation: descendant in the male line of Louis De Geer, founder of the Swedish Africa Company
today_people.role: Artist and filmmaker; made the exhibition 'Släkten och slavarna' (The Family and the Slaves, Norrköping 2018 and Stockholm) on his family's slave-trade past

records.name: De Geer family (Louis & Laurens De Geer)
records.scaleNote: Financed and founded the Swedish Africa Company (1649), a small player in the Gold Coast trade.
records.origins: Louis De Geer, a Liège-born Calvinist merchant in Amsterdam, became Sweden's leading industrialist in iron and armaments. His sister Maria married the Amsterdam arms merchant Elias Trip, linking the De Geers to the Trip family.
records.role_summary: With his son Laurens, Louis De Geer founded the Swedish Africa Company in 1649 and financed its Gold Coast expedition. The family's Swedish iron and guns were key goods in Atlantic trade.

roleDetail.t: Dutch capital under a Swedish flag.
roleDetail.d: De Geer used Swedish charters to enter a trade the Dutch WIC monopolised at home.
The Trip–De Geer arms network supplied guns and metals traded across the Atlantic world; no direct Trip slave-trading has been confirmed here.

records.legacy: The De Geers remain a prominent Swedish noble family. The Trippenhuis in Amsterdam, built by Trip relatives in 1662, now houses the Royal Netherlands Academy of Arts and Sciences.

legacyDetail.d: Finspång and other De Geer works remain landmarks of Swedish industry.

lineage.name: Louys de Geer
lineage.note: Walloon merchant from Liège who moved the family to Dordrecht in the Dutch Republic for religious reasons.

lineage.name: Louis De Geer
lineage.note: Armaments and iron magnate in Sweden, ennobled in 1640, who backed the 1646 Africa voyage and the 1649 Swedish Africa Company.

lineage.name: Adrienne Gérard
lineage.note: Wife of Louis; the couple had 16 children, who formed the Dutch and Swedish branches.

lineage.name: Laurens De Geer
lineage.note: Co-founder and Amsterdam commissioner of the Swedish Africa Company; in 1657 he contracted to sell 500–600 captives to be bought on the Guinea coast.

lineage.name: Louis De Geer the younger & Emanuel De Geer
lineage.note: Louis the younger took over Finspång; Emanuel received Leufsta in 1650. Leufsta stayed with the family for about 13 generations before passing to the Swedish state.

lineage.name: Louis Gerhard De Geer & Gerhard Louis De Geer
lineage.note: Father and son, each Prime Minister of Sweden (1876–80 and 1920–21).

lineage.name: Carl Johan De Geer
lineage.note: Artist who in 2014 held an exhibition on his ancestor Louis's role in Swedish industry and the slave trade.

records.today: The De Geer family has Swedish and Dutch branches that still exist, some members holding the title of baron, and it produced two Swedish prime ministers. The artist Carl Johan De Geer has spoken publicly about the family link and held a 2014 exhibition on Louis De Geer's role in the slave trade. Leufsta bruk, the family's ironworks seat for generations, is now managed by the Swedish state. Carl Johan De Geer's exhibition 'Släkten och slavarna' (The Family and the Slaves) was shown in Norrköping in 2018 and later in Stockholm.

today_people.relation: descendant in the male line of Louis De Geer, founder of the Swedish Africa Company

records.name: Hendrik Carloff
records.scaleNote: A company agent who served the Dutch, Swedish and Danish Gold Coast ventures in turn; important for founding forts rather than for the number of captives he shipped.
records.origins: A Rostock-born merchant who served the Dutch WIC on the Gold Coast before offering his knowledge to the Swedish De Geer venture.
records.role_summary: Carloff led the Swedish expedition of 1650 and built Carolusborg. After leaving Swedish service he became director of the Danish Africa Company (1657–1662) and in 1658 seized the Swedish posts for Denmark.

roleDetail.d: His capture of Carolusborg for Denmark in January 1658 showed how agents moved between rival companies.

records.legacy: Carloff's career shows how small states entered the Gold Coast trade through Dutch-trained agents.

legacyDetail.d: Leiden researchers have studied Carloff as a transimperial broker.

lineage.name: Dutch West India Company
lineage.note: Carloff rose from soldier and clerk in Dutch Brazil to WIC service on the Gold Coast at Elmina and Fort Nassau.

lineage.name: Louis & Laurens De Geer
lineage.note: Laurens hired him in Amsterdam in 1649 as director and commandant of the Swedish Africa Company; he was knighted in Sweden in 1654.

lineage.name: Danish (Glückstadt) Africa Company
lineage.note: As director-general he captured Carolusborg for Denmark in 1658 and was made governor of the Glückstadt company in 1659.

lineage.name: French West India Company (Colbert)
lineage.note: Led slaving voyages to Angola and the French Antilles, and was named a counsellor of the company by Colbert in 1665.

lineage.name: Sophia Felicitas von Wolzogen
lineage.note: His wife, from a German noble family; no children are recorded.

records.today: No publicly documented descendants have been traced. Carloff's last recorded post was governor of Tobago (1676–77), where he was taken into custody after the French capture, and his fortune is not documented after that.

records.name: Duke Jacob Kettler and the Duchy of Courland
records.scaleNote: Courland held St Andrew's Island in the Gambia (1651–1661) and Tobago intermittently; its role in the slave trade was small and is poorly documented.
records.origins: Ruler of a small Baltic duchy under Polish-Lithuanian overlordship, Jacob built a large merchant fleet and sought colonies after Dutch and English models.
records.role_summary: He leased St Andrew's Island in the Gambia from the Kingdom of Niumi in 1651 and built Fort Jacob, and planted 'New Courland' on Tobago from 1654. The Gambia fort traded in gold, ivory and some captives; most were taken by the Dutch and English while Jacob was a Swedish prisoner (1658–1660).

roleDetail.d: St Andrew's Island, later James Island, became an English slave-trading fort after 1661.
How many captives Courland itself shipped is unclear; sources mostly emphasise trade goods.

records.legacy: St Andrew's/James Island is now Kunta Kinteh Island, a UNESCO World Heritage site. In Latvia the colonies are often a point of national pride, which historians are starting to question.

legacyDetail.d: The Gambian island Courland first fortified was renamed in 2011 after the character in Roots.

lineage.name: Gotthard Kettler
lineage.note: Last Master of the Livonian Order, who made himself first Duke of Courland and Semigallia in 1561 under Polish suzerainty.

lineage.name: Wilhelm Kettler & Sophie of Prussia
lineage.note: Jacob's parents; through his mother he was tied to the Hohenzollern dynasty.

lineage.name: Louise Charlotte of Brandenburg
lineage.note: Daughter of Elector George William and sister of the Great Elector, who later founded Brandenburg's own African company.

lineage.name: Frederick Casimir Kettler
lineage.note: Succeeded in 1682 as Courland's colonial footholds in the Gambia and Tobago fell away.

lineage.name: Ferdinand Kettler
lineage.note: Last Kettler duke; he died without issue in 1737 and the male line ended.

lineage.name: Russian Empire
lineage.note: Russia annexed Courland in the Third Partition of Poland; it is now part of Latvia.

records.today: The male Kettler line died out in 1737; Jacob's descendants through his daughters married into the Hesse-Homburg and Hesse-Kassel houses. Jacob is buried in the ducal crypt of Jelgava Palace in Latvia, where the colonies are often a point of national pride. St Andrew's Island in the Gambia is now Kunta Kinteh Island, a UNESCO World Heritage site.

records.name: Crédit Industriel et Commercial (CIC)
records.scaleNote: Not a slave trader, but the bank that profited most from Haiti's 1875 loan, taken to keep paying the 1825 'independence debt' (per the New York Times 'Ransom' investigation, 2022).
records.origins: A Paris bank founded in 1859, now part of Crédit Mutuel Alliance Fédérale.
records.role_summary: In 1875 CIC arranged a loan to Haiti whose fees and interest drained the Haitian treasury; it also helped found Haiti's national bank, which was controlled from Paris.

roleDetail.d: The 1825 indemnity plus loans to pay it cost Haiti c. 112 million francs, about $560 million today, and an estimated $21–115 billion in lost growth (NYT).
CIC helped set up the Banque Nationale d'Haïti, which was run from Paris and drew profits from Haiti's treasury (NYT, 2022).

records.legacy: The NYT series renewed calls for France to return the indemnity. In 2025, the bicentenary of the debt, France set up a joint commission of historians.

legacyDetail.d: The Collège de France held a symposium 'Haiti 1825: from independence to debt'.

lineage.name: Armand Donon & the Duke of Morny
lineage.note: Founded the Société générale de crédit industriel et commercial on 7 May 1859 as a rival to the Pereires' Crédit Mobilier.

lineage.name: Haiti loans & Banque Nationale d'Haïti
lineage.note: CIC arranged the 1875 loan of 50 million francs, of which Haiti's treasury netted about 7 million from the first tranche, set up the Paris-controlled national bank in 1880–81 and was involved in a further 50 million-franc loan in 1896; its role ended around 1910.

lineage.name: Suez group / French state
lineage.note: Nationalised in 1982 under Mitterrand along with its parent, the Suez Company.

lineage.name: GAN (insurer)
lineage.note: The state insurer GAN built up a stake that reached 92.6% by 1995.

lineage.name: Crédit Mutuel (Banque Fédérative du Crédit Mutuel)
lineage.note: Won the 1998 privatisation tender for 67% of CIC, later took full ownership, and delisted it in 2017.

records.today: CIC is now wholly owned by the Crédit Mutuel group, one of France's five biggest banking groups; Nicolas Théry has chaired it since 2014. The 2022 New York Times investigation 'The Ransom' estimated that French shareholders made at least $136 million in today's money from the Haitian national bank over three decades, and CIC faced international controversy as a result. As a corporate institution, CIC has no family descendants.

records.name: Nantes
records.description: France's leading slave-trading port: Nantes outfitted c. 1,744 slaving expeditions, about 41% of the French total, and its ships deported more than 500,000 Africans in the 18th century (per Wikipedia summarising Nantes-based research). Merchant houses such as the Montaudoins built the Feydeau and Île Gloriette mansions on these profits.

records.name: Bordeaux
records.description: France's second slave port by many measures, with c. 508 slave-trading expeditions deporting an estimated 120,000–150,000 Africans between 1672 and 1837, and France's main port for colonial sugar and coffee. The Musée d'Aquitaine opened permanent rooms on the slave trade in 2009, and street plaques now explain names such as rue Gradis.

records.name: La Rochelle
records.description: A leading French slave port (often ranked second or third), with an estimated c. 130,000 Africans deported on its ships, mainly to the French Antilles and Saint-Domingue, where many of its shipowners also held plantations. The Musée du Nouveau Monde occupies the Hôtel Fleuriau, built for a planter-merchant family.

records.name: Le Havre
records.description: A major Normandy slave port in the 18th century and a centre of illegal French slaving after 1815, as in the 1819 voyage of Le Rôdeur to Guadeloupe. A plaque near the port remembers the c. 90,000 Africans trafficked on Le Havre ships, and the Maison de l'Armateur and Hôtel Dubocage de Bléville hold exhibitions on the trade.

records.name: Amsterdam
records.description: The financial heart of the Dutch Atlantic: seat of the WIC's main chamber, one-third owner of the Society of Suriname (1683–1795), and home of banks such as Hope & Co. that lent to slave plantations. On 1 July 2021 Mayor Femke Halsema apologised for the city government's 'active involvement' in colonial slavery.

records.name: Saint-Domingue (colonial Haiti)
records.description: France's richest colony and the world's largest sugar and coffee producer by the 1780s, with c. 465,000 enslaved people in 1789, about two-thirds of them born in Africa. The revolution that began in August 1791 ended slavery and created independent Haiti on 1 January 1804, the first state founded by formerly enslaved people.

records.name: Code Noir (1685)
records.description: Edict of Louis XIV issued at Versailles in March 1685, in 60 articles, regulating slavery in the French colonies: it imposed Catholicism, expelled Jews, defined enslaved people as movable property and set punishments, while nominally limiting masters' power. It was extended to Saint-Domingue and later Louisiana and stayed largely in force until 1848.

records.name: Gorée Island
records.description: A small island off Dakar held in turn by the Portuguese, Dutch, English and French, and a French slave-trading base under the Senegal companies. It became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1978; the claim that millions passed through its 'House of Slaves' is disputed by historians such as Philip Curtin, who estimate far smaller numbers (some cite c. 26,000 recorded), but it is widely accepted as a memorial site.

records.name: Curaçao
records.description: Taken from Spain by the WIC in 1634, Curaçao became the main Dutch depot for selling captives on to Spanish America, especially under asiento contracts from 1662 and illegally thereafter; it may have delivered c. 100,000 people to Spanish colonies. Willemstad's Kura Hulanda museum and the 1795 Tula revolt are central to its memory today.

records.name: Sint Eustatius
records.description: A small Dutch island that became a free port and, after the mid-18th century, the main Dutch transit point for captives sold on to neighbouring colonies, overtaking Curaçao (per SlaveVoyages). A slave depot stood within the Waterfort.

records.name: New Amsterdam (New Netherland)
records.description: The WIC's settlement on Manhattan, where enslaved Africans arrived from c. 1626 and built Fort Amsterdam. In 1644 eleven company-owned men won 'half-freedom' and land north of the town. The English took the colony in 1664 and renamed it New York.

records.name: Society of Suriname
records.description: Founded in 1683 and owned in equal thirds by the city of Amsterdam, the Van Aerssen van Sommelsdijck family and the WIC to run Suriname. By 1713 c. 13,000 enslaved Africans worked c. 200 plantations producing sugar, coffee and cocoa for Amsterdam; Suriname received about 40% of all captives landed by the Dutch. Dissolved in 1795.

records.name: Christiansborg Castle (Osu Castle), Accra
records.description: Denmark-Norway's main Gold Coast fort at Osu, taken over in the late 1650s and the base for Danish slave purchases. Akwamu forces captured it in 1693 and held it for a year. Sold to Britain in 1850, it later served as Ghana's seat of government.

records.name: Fredensborg (slave ship, 1768)
records.description: A Danish-Norwegian slave ship that embarked c. 265 captives on the Gold Coast and landed 235 on St Croix in 1768, then sank off Tromøy near Arendal, Norway, on its return. Found in 1974, it is one of the very few excavated slave ships; its finds are held by the Aust-Agder museum.

records.name: Groß Friedrichsburg
records.description: Brandenburg's fort at Princes Town, Ghana, begun on 1 January 1683 and the base of its slave trading. Sold to the Dutch WIC by an agreement of 1717; local ally John Conny held it until 1724, after which the Dutch renamed it Fort Hollandia.

records.name: Carolusborg (Cape Coast)
records.description: Fort founded by the Swedish Africa Company at Cabo Corso in 1650–53 with the king of Fetu's consent. Captured by the Danes in 1658 and the Dutch in 1663, it was taken by the English in 1664 and rebuilt as Cape Coast Castle.

records.name: Danish West Indies (St Thomas, St John, St Croix)
records.description: Denmark-Norway's Caribbean sugar colonies: St Thomas from 1672, St John from 1718 and St Croix, bought from France in 1733. Enslaved people revolted on St John in 1733 and forced emancipation on St Croix on 3 July 1848. Sold to the US in 1917; now the US Virgin Islands.

records.name: Haiti's 'independence debt' (1825 indemnity)
records.description: Under naval threat, Charles X's 1825 ordinance made France's recognition of Haiti conditional on 150 million francs to compensate former colonists, including for enslaved 'property'; it was reduced in 1838. Haiti borrowed from French banks to pay. The NYT (2022) found Haiti paid c. 112 million francs (c. $560 million today) through 1947, at an estimated cost of $21–115 billion in lost growth.

records.name: Taubira Law (2001)
records.description: French Law no. 2001-434 of 21 May 2001, drafted by Christiane Taubira, deputy for French Guiana, recognised the Atlantic and Indian Ocean slave trades and slavery as crimes against humanity. It required them to be taught in schools and led to a national remembrance day (10 May).

records.name: Danish slave-trade decree (1792)
records.description: Signed by Christian VII on 16 March 1792 after a commission chaired by Ernst Schimmelmann, it banned the import of captives into the Danish West Indies and their export from Danish forts in Guinea, but only from 1803. It did not end slavery, which lasted until 1848.

records.name: Mémorial de l'abolition de l'esclavage, Nantes
records.description: Opened on 25 March 2012 on the Quai de la Fosse, the memorial has c. 2,000 glass inserts, about 1,710 of them naming Nantes slave-ship expeditions and their dates. It is one of Europe's largest memorials to the slave trade.

records.name: Compagnie de Guinée (Asiento company)
records.description: French chartered company with the monopoly on the slave trade from Sierra Leone to the Cape of Good Hope. In 1701 Philip V of Spain gave it the asiento to supply captives to Spanish America, which passed to Britain's South Sea Company at the 1713 Treaty of Utrecht.

records.name: Compagnie du Sénégal
records.description: Successive French chartered companies (from 1673) that ran Saint-Louis and Gorée with a monopoly from Cap Blanc to the Sierra Leone river, trading gum, gold and captives. The monopoly passed to the Compagnie des Indes in December 1718.

records.name: Hope & Co.
records.description: An Amsterdam merchant bank founded by the Hope family, one of Europe's leading houses in the 18th century. IISH research (2022) found it lent to at least 73 Caribbean plantations with enslaved people as security, and drew c. 25–33% of revenue from slavery in sample years. It is a legal predecessor of ABN AMRO.

records.name: Courland colonies: St Andrew's Island (Gambia) and New Courland (Tobago)
records.description: The Duchy of Courland leased St Andrew's Island in the Gambia River from the Kingdom of Niumi in 1651 and built Fort Jacob, and planted 'New Courland' on Tobago from 1654. The Gambia fort fell to the Dutch and then the English (1661), becoming James Island, today Kunta Kinteh Island.
